same_study_reason: Both lists discuss a small forecasting exercise about cultured-meat scale-up, its elicitation questions, techno-economic cost inputs, and aggregate forecasts.

pairs.reason: Both concern techno-economic analyses used to anchor forecast materials, especially cost assumptions. A1 identifies a specific FGF2 units/scenario error; B1 criticises the broader anchoring and synthesis approach rather than that numerical error.

Both flag errors in the materials for an input-cost question. A1 concerns the FGF2/Delft units and zero-price scenario; B2 concerns the category and reference wording that mixes recombinant proteins with non-amino-acid examples.

Both identify interpretive problems created by multi-condition elicitation questions. A2 is a specific case in which conditional acceptance evidence is presented as unconditional; B10 is the broader critique of compound thresholds, price conditions, time windows, and restrictions.

Both concern underspecified definitions in cultured-meat forecast questions. A3 concerns the species and tissue/cell type for beef questions, whereas B3 concerns the measurement basis for a 51%-animal-cells construct.

A3 gives a specific example of inadequate question definition producing divergent interpretations; B10 more broadly identifies complex and restricted question wording as a source of interpretation variance.

Both warn that claims drawn from six respondents can overstate what the data support. B5 applies this to correlation significance and multiple testing, while A4 more generally challenges inference about forecaster disagreement and group differences.

Both identify the very small forecasting panel as insufficient for strong aggregate or comparative conclusions. B6 is broader, adding representativeness, calibration, uncertainty, and individual-forecaster sensitivity.

Both concern how a tiny panel is represented in aggregate forecasts. A4 says aggregate reporting conceals disagreement; B7 challenges the particular geometric-odds pooling rule and its sensitivity to outliers.

Both criticise reliance on a narrow set of techno-economic analyses as forecasting background. A5 focuses on overreliance on Humbird and insufficient breadth/recency; B1 broadens this to the absent framework for combining engineering and reference-class evidence.
Both criticise the forecasting-panel design. A5 concerns the lack of discussion and updating among participants, while B6 concerns panel size, representativeness, calibration, and sensitivity.

Both concern the role and interpretation of techno-economic analyses in the forecast background. A6 says conditional and present-cost scenarios are misleadingly presented as predictions; B1 challenges the anchoring and integration framework.

Both flag biologically inaccurate or confused categorisation of media-input concepts in the forecast materials. A6 is the broader critique of erroneous growth-factor definitions and missing expertise; B2 specifies a recombinant-protein/non-amino-acid wording error in one cost question.
